Builds sign ad-hoc Every worker gets: Variable Value Effect XCODE_XCCONFIG_FILE <state>/worker-guard/worker.xcconfig (macOS) Xcode builds (also through other build tools that call it) sign to run locally: CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY = - , CODE_SIGN_STYLE = Manual , no team or provisioning profile. Xcode applies the file above every target's settings, so no identity is searched and no keychain opened. APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY - App bundlers that read it (Tauri among them) sign ad-hoc. GCM_INTERACTIVE never A git credential helper never opens a sign-in window. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT 0 git never waits for a user name or password in the terminal. Signing and notarising with a real identity belong to the release process, not to a worker. The worker brief says so ( SIGNING_RULE in crates/core/src/orchestration/brief.rs ): build unsigned or ad-hoc, never touch keychains, certificates or trust settings, and when signing is left out, say so in the result. 2. security and codesign go through a guard (macOS) The folder <state>/worker-guard comes first on the worker's PATH and holds two small scripts, security and codesign , that run gitoodo keychain-guard <tool> … . The guard reads the search list and the default keychain ( security list-keychains , default-keychain ), asks each keychain the call can reach whether it is locked (with user interaction switched off for its own process, so the question itself never opens a dialog), and then: Refuses with a reason for the worker what would need a locked keychain: settings or contents of a named locked keychain, writing into a locked default keychain, and any other call that names no keychain while one in the search list is locked. Refuses always what asks a person: unlock-keychain and create-keychain without -p , any -P (password through a dialog), set-keychain-password , trust settings changes ( add-trusted-cert , remove-trusted-cert , …), authorizationdb changes, authorize , interactive mode -i . Skips locked keychains in searches that take keychains as arguments ( find-generic-password , find-internet-password , their delete- forms, dump-keychain ): the unlocked keychains of the search list are passed explicitly. An agent reading its own login from the login keychain keeps working while another keychain is locked. Signs only from unlocked keychains : codesign -s <identity> (not - ) with a locked keychain in the search list looks the identity up in the unlocked ones ( security find-identity , which never opens a keychain) and signs with --keychain <that one> ; if only a locked keychain has it, the call is refused. codesign --keychain <locked> is refused. Runs unchanged what cannot open a keychain: listing keychains, certificate and identity searches, verifying and displaying signatures, ad-hoc signing, lock-keychain . Stopped when a dialog still appears Some dialogs cannot be foreseen: an unlocked keychain can still ask whether a program may use an item. The guard runs the tool as its child; when a keychain dialog process ( SecurityAgent ) appears that was not running when the call started and the call is still running after three seconds, the guard ends the call, closes that dialog process (otherwise its dialog stays on the screen after the caller is gone; macOS starts it again for the next request) and tells the worker: signing needs a keychain, build unsigned or ad-hoc. A dialog process that was already running is someone else's; then the guard does not interfere. Limits Tools that call /usr/bin/security or /usr/bin/codesign by their full path bypass the scripts. Xcode does, which is why its builds sign ad-hoc through the override file instead. A worker's shell that rebuilds PATH from scratch in its startup files loses the folder. Startup files that only put folders in front keep it working, since those folders hold neither tool. Linux and Windows have no such keychain dialogs from these tools; workers there get only the environment variables. Checked on a real Mac In the desktop session of a worker machine, with throwaway keychains (one locked with a self-signed code signing identity, one unlocked with an item that trusts no application), through the guard: security show-keychain-info <locked> and codesign --keychain <locked> -s … were refused in under a second without a dialog; codesign -s <identity only in the locked keychain> was refused; certificate searches in the locked keychain, the agent's login read, ad-hoc signing and verifying ran as before; reading the item that trusts no application was stopped after three seconds and its dialog closed. Without the guard the same show-keychain-info call opened a password dialog and hung.

h: When the inputs cannot go there
Fetching more while the worker runs
Data is never a missing command
b: Some issues need files that git does not carry: a git-ignored data folder, an untracked note, the transcript of an earlier agent session. They exist only on the machine where someone prepared them, usually the main host. A worker on another machine would not find them and would ask a person to copy them. Gitoodo brings them instead, so no person ever copies files for the autopilot (#1582). Implemented in crates/core/src/inputs/ (lookup, placement, transfer format), the dispatcher's side in crates/cli/src/dispatcher_inputs.rs and the worker machine's side in crates/cli/src/satellite.rs ( inputs_receive , place_inputs ). What counts as an input The issue body names them; nothing has to be declared elsewhere. Paths in inline code , relative to the repository: `.scratch/research/data/txt/` , `notes/plan.md` . A path relative to the folder of another named input counts too ( `data/meta.tsv` next to `.scratch/research/data/txt/` ). Absolute and home paths, URLs, globs, .. and .git are never inputs; fenced code blocks are not read. Agent session transcripts by their id : any <uuid>.jsonl in the body. The main host looks for projects/*/<uuid>.jsonl below the Claude Code folder ( CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR , else ~/.claude ) and sessions/**/rollout-…-<uuid>.jsonl below the Codex folder ( CODEX_HOME , else ~/.codex ). The path as written belongs to the machine that wrote it and is not used; the id is the explicit reference. Gitoodo's own log files as `log:<file>` : `log:dispatcher.jsonl` (#1411), so a worker anywhere can analyse the dispatcher's production log of the main host. Only a plain file name in Gitoodo's log folder of the main host counts ( <process>.jsonl , <process>-<pid>.jsonl , gitoodo.log , each also rotated with .1 … .N ; a bare log:dispatcher means dispatcher.jsonl ); no folder, path, glob, .lock or stderr file ( log_name ). A current file comes with its rotated generations, so the hours before the last rotation come too; a rotated name ( log:dispatcher.jsonl.2 ) is that file alone. They land in .gitoodo-inputs/logs/<file> . Logs never hold a token (see security ), so they may go where the issue's worker runs, like a transcript. No other file outside the repository is ever read. Only the issue body counts, not comments: issues reach a worker only from trusted authors (see security ), comments can come from anyone. Files for every worker Some files every worker of a repository needs: a local .env , a git-ignored test data folder, a local config. Settings → the repository → Workers → "Files for every worker" lists them once instead of every issue naming them (#1583; worktree_files in the repository's entry of orchestration.json , set with set_repo_worktree_files ). Paths relative to the repository, a bare folder name ( fixtures ) too; no globs, no absolute or home paths, no .. or .git , at most 32 ( normalize_repo_files ). The field takes one entry per line, commas separate too (a blank stays part of its entry and is refused, so test data never becomes two paths). It checks them by these rules before storing and names the first wrong entry and why, instead of a bare "Saving failed" (#1621, src/views/settings/worktreeFiles.ts ). Under the field the settings name the listed paths missing from the repository's working copy on this computer, since a worker only gets what lies there ( repo_worktree_files_missing ; nothing while there is no working copy). They are looked up, placed and sent with the issue's own inputs on every start, resolver run and move, by the same rules and limits; what both name counts once. A file named like a credential is taken only when the list names its exact path ( .env , not the folder holding it). It then reaches worker machines too: list it only when every worker may read it. Logs name counts, never paths or contents. Lookup on the main host The dispatcher resolves the named inputs when a worker starts ( begin ), in the main host's working copy of the repository (the copy worktrees are cut from, local_copy ): A path must exist, lie inside the copy after resolving it ( canonicalize ), and not be a symlink. Folders are read to a depth of 32; symlinks, .git and nested repositories inside them are skipped. What git tracks is in the worktree anyway and is left out ( git ls-files ). A file named like a credential ( .env* , keys, key stores, credentials.json , the agents' own sign-in files, anything in .ssh ) is never an input, unless the repository's list of files for every worker names its exact path (see below). The worker's brief names what was left out, so it can say so instead of guessing. Limits: at most 20,000 files and 1 GiB for a worker machine ( MAX_FILES , MAX_TOTAL_BYTES ). A worker on the main host gets every file (only the file count cuts). Where the inputs land A file git ignores keeps its path, so the worker finds it where the issue says. Anything else (a session transcript, an untracked file outside an ignored folder) lands below .gitoodo-inputs/ ( sessions/<uuid>.jsonl , files/<path> ). That folder holds a .gitignore with * , so it ignores itself and everything in it. So no input ever shows in git status or ends up in a commit. A file already in the worktree stays as it is (a restarted worker may have changed it). Transfer to a worker machine Over the satellite connection the repository copy already uses ( satellites.md , "Own copies"), right after the copy and before the spawn: The main host packs the inputs into one archive (8-byte length, a JSON list of {dest, size} , then the bytes) in a temporary file and computes its SHA-256. inputs_receive ( Request::InputsReceive {cwd, size, sha256} ) is followed by the archive in chunks of 512 KiB (base64), as for the copy. The worker machine checks the size, the checksum, every path (relative, no .. , no .git , no drive letter, no duplicates) and that the sizes add up, and unpacks into its staging folder ( <state>/inputs/<hash of the worktree path> ). The worktree does not exist yet. spawn creates the worktree as before and then moves the staged files in ( satellite.inputs_placed ). Staging left behind by a start that never came is removed after a day. The worker machine never reads a path of the main host and never asks for a file: it only takes what the main host sends. The token is in no archive, frame or log line; logs name counts and sizes, never file contents. When the inputs cannot go there Too large for a worker machine, or the transfer fails ( RemoteStart::Inputs ): the start there ends without a machine fault ( dispatch.inputs_local ), the lease is released and the issue gets the label host:<this computer> , the same label a person sets to pin an issue to a machine. It then runs on the main host, which has the data. The label stays visible on the forge and is removed like any host: label. A worker machine taking up its update first ( outdated ) is held as for the copy; the issue starts where there is room. Resolver runs and moves A resolver run on a stuck issue and a run moved to another machine for its desktop tests get the same inputs as the issue's first run (#1585): copied into the worktree here, or sent along to the worker machine. A set too large to send is left out there; the brief then says to hand the issue back with gitoodo worker needs --data . Fetching more while the worker runs gitoodo worker input PATH copies a further local file or folder of the main host into the worktree: a path relative to the repository, or a session transcript <id>.jsonl , by the same rules as in an issue body (#1584), or a log file of Gitoodo ( log:dispatcher.jsonl , #1411). A worker on the main host asks the dispatcher's broker, which looks the path up in the working copy and copies it in. A worker on a worker machine asks its satellite service, which forwards the request on the main host's subscription ( Reply::InputForward , like gitoodo worker context ). The main host checks that the machine holds the issue's lease, looks the path up, sends the files over a connection of its own ( inputs_receive , as at the start) and confirms ( Request::InputDone ); the service then places them in the worktree and answers the worker ( Reply::Delivered ). What is not there, is a credential or is larger than a worker machine is sent comes back as a reason the worker can act on; nothing is copied. Data is never a missing command A worker once reported missing data as a missing command ( gitoodo worker needs --tool youtube-research-data ). The issue got a tool: label no machine could ever satisfy and waited for a person. Three things keep that from happening again: ** gitoodo worker needs --data PATH --reason "why" ** hands the issue back for local files: from a worker machine the issue goes to the main host ( host: label, result needs_data ) and never gets a tool: label. A worker on the main host is not handed back at all: the broker copies what it finds and tells the worker to go on without the rest. --data takes the same paths as worker input , so a word like youtube-research-data is refused there as well. A log of the main host counts as data too: needs --data log:dispatcher.jsonl hands an issue that needs the production logs to the main host, where an absolute path like ~/Library/Logs/<id>/dispatcher.jsonl would be refused and the worker would be stuck (#1411). Main host first for unknown commands: a --tool hand-back from a worker machine for a command that no machine is known to have (this computer is probed afresh, worker machines by their last probe) also goes to the main host instead of becoming a tool: label ( needs_here ). The person's own computer has their files and their setup; only when a worker there hands the issue back for the same command does it get the label, and with it the "Install it or run without" line on "Asked of me". Hand-back marks still end after 24 hours. The brief says that --tool names programs only, never data, files or folders, and names worker input and needs --data . What the worker is told Every worker brief carries the rule ( brief::INPUTS_RULE ): Gitoodo copies the files the issue names before the start; never ask a person to copy files onto this machine; a named file that is missing was not found on the main host either, so do what is possible without it, say so in the result and ask only how to go on without it. When there are inputs, the brief starts with a section Local inputs that lists each one with its place in the worktree, size and file count.

When the autopilot gives up on an issue (label stalled , see docs/states.md ), the resolver tries it once before a person is asked: one run of a coding agent that finds why the issue is stuck, removes the blocker and goes on with the issue's branch and pull request like a worker. If that does not work, the person gets a normal question in the question format ( docs/question-format.md ) with the cause, what was tried, the options and a recommendation. The code is crates/core/src/resolver.rs (record, decision, prompt, question, note) and crates/cli/src/dispatcher_resolver.rs (trigger, start, outcome). When it runs The resolver is triggered the moment the dispatcher marks an issue stalled . The stall notice waits meanwhile: the person hears of the issue only when the resolver asks. One attempt per stuck issue, never a loop. A resolver run never stalls an issue again and never starts a second run for the same stall. When the resolver got an issue moving and it gets stuck again within 7 days, the person is asked right away. Only a new conflict, failed update or moving base after it got the issue moving (the base moved on, nothing for a person to decide) is resolved again, up to 3 times in a row ( again in the record), before the person is asked (#1564). A resolver run cut off twice by a restart of the dispatcher is not started a third time. Ahead of new issues, within the total. Waiting resolver attempts take the next free slot before any new issue, up to the system slots (see "System slots" below). They count in "workers at once" like any run, never on top of it (#1531), and a machine's own maximum always holds. A running worker is never stopped for them. One that finds no place within an hour asks the person instead. It goes through the same usage gate as a worker: a login whose usage is known spent, or not known where "pause on unknown usage" holds (Codex always without a worker distribution), takes no resolver run either. Only where the autopilot works. Never in a paused or hidden repository; an attempt waiting when the autopilot is paused is dropped (the issue stays stuck, nothing is asked). Hands off an issue that is labelled extern , has a session of a person open, or has an open question to a person ( needs-human ), and one that is no longer stalled when its turn comes. Out of an agent's reach (a sign-in on the worker's machine) means no run: the person is asked at once, with the fix in the question. A working copy held by another run gets no resolver either; that cause passes by itself and "Try again" stays the way out. A full disk holds it like any new local work (the disk guard): this computer takes no attempt, a worker machine with room still does. With none, waiting attempts stay queued, and their hour of waiting starts again once there is space, so nobody is asked about a full disk. The backlog sweep The trigger misses stalls that happened before the resolver existed, while the dispatcher was down, or in a crash between the label and the record. A sweep catches them: once at the dispatcher's start and then every ten minutes by the clock, independent of the stall trigger. It looks at every stalled issue and queues an attempt for each whose recorded stall ( stall.json ) has none yet, with the same rules as above (switches, Autopilot, hands off, out of reach asks at once). A stall younger than five minutes is left to its trigger. Each sweep logs one line, resolver.sweep , with what it found, queued and asked, how many records it wrote ( recorded ) and the skipped issues by reason. Stuck without a record: an issue that was stuck before the dispatcher kept stall records has no recorded cause. The sweep writes one for it ( stall.json , cause unknown , logged as resolver.stall_recorded ): stalled when the issue last changed on the forge (a label change moves that time too), or at the sweep when the forge does not answer, never older than 30 days. From then on it is a stall like any other: younger than five minutes it waits for the next sweep, and it gets exactly one attempt. The run's brief says the cause is unknown and has it work the cause out first: the issue and its comments, the branch against its base, an open pull request with its state and checks ( gitoodo worker context ), the worktree, and the dispatcher's log of the issue ( gitoodo trace <owner/repo>#<n> ); then it acts as for that cause. The question after a failed attempt names the cause as "not recorded". An issue the resolver already had is never recorded again, even when its stall record is gone. Attempts from the sweep are the backlog , started after the fresh stalls, oldest stall first, in the system slots like fresh ones. Beyond those, the backlog takes the slots the round's new work left free. There is no further share for a large backlog: it would come out of the user's own worker slots, and the two system slots already give it a start in every round in which a slot frees. The disk guard holds the backlog like any new local work. No question is asked for the wait, so a long backlog never turns into a flood of questions. The stuck list says "The resolver takes it as soon as a slot is free" on such a row and counts the issues the resolver works through under its heading. A pause drops backlog attempts that have not begun (the next sweep after the pause queues them again). Never twice: an issue whose record holds this stall in any state (resolved, asked, skipped, stopped, or still waiting or running) is never swept again for it. Only a later stall is new. Switches: Settings → Dispatcher → "Resolver for stuck issues" (global, dispatch.resolver , on by default) and per repository the rule "Resolver for stuck issues" next to the Autopilot (on by default while the Autopilot is on). Either switch off means no attempt. System slots Of the slots of "workers at once", up to two go first to the resolver's runs, the **system slots** ( gitoodo_core::system_slots ; dispatch.system_slots in the config file, no setting in the app; 0 lets them wait like new issues). They are a priority, not capacity of their own: every resolver run counts in the total and goes through the same gate as every start ( docs/orchestrator/dispatcher.md , "One gate"), and each machine's own maximum holds. While every slot is busy, a waiting attempt takes the next one that frees, ahead of new issues. Until #1531 the system slots came on top of the total, which let the fleet run "9 of 8". Only while needed. While no resolver attempt waits or runs, the workers use every slot of the total. When one comes, nothing running is stopped; it starts in a system slot on any machine with room below its own maximum. Kept at the start (#1422). Until every repository with the autopilot on or a resolver attempt was read in this run (or the first full poll is done), the system slots take no new issue, so a waiting attempt is not overtaken by workers in the first minute. Attempts from resolver.json start once their repository was read in this run, not on the stored model, so no decision rests on old labels; the classifier reads those repositories first. With no need known, the slots go back to the workers at once ( dispatch.system_reserve_start / _end ). Any machine for the resolver. A resolver run goes to any machine with a free slot within its own maximum, chosen with the same checks as a worker's (sign-in, agent, tools, the issue's os: and host: labels), the machine it stalled on first, since its working copy is there. Triage takes no slot (#1426). A triage call is a short model call of the classifier on the dispatcher's computer, one at a time, without a working copy. It neither waits for a slot nor counts against a machine's maximum or the total, so new issues are assessed right away even while every slot runs a worker. A running call is marked ( triage-call in the state folder, older than two minutes holds nothing) for the status page only. The status page keeps this calm: the Resolver line says how many system slots are in use only on hover ("System slots: 1 of 2 in use"). The run The resolver runs on any machine with a free slot (see "System slots"), the one the issue stuck on first; the question after a failed attempt names that machine. It prefers an agent of the worker pool other than the one that got stuck. Its worktree is set up from the issue's branch, so it continues where the workers stopped. On a worker machine it reads its context ( gitoodo worker context ) and delivers like a worker there, through the dispatcher's computer, which holds the forge token. Its prompt names only commands that work there: a wait for other issues is a question ( gitoodo ask ) instead of gitoodo worker blocked , which only the dispatcher's computer records, and gitoodo trace shows that machine's part of the log. A question there leaves the attempt waiting for the answer as on this computer. A machine that ends its waiting runs for an update puts the attempt back into the queue without costing a start; it starts again in a free slot like any waiting one. Its first message holds the issue, the recorded stall cause, the run history, the end of the last run's output, the conflicting files for a conflict, and the worktree and branch. It tells the agent to diagnose, fix and end with one machine-readable outcome: Outcome Command Fixed and delivered (push, PR) gitoodo worker resolved --reason <text> The blocker passed, a worker goes on gitoodo worker resolved --requeue --reason <text> The base already does it gitoodo worker resolved --obsolete <sha> --reason <text> Waits for other issues gitoodo worker blocked --on #N --reason <text> Only a person can decide or act gitoodo ask (a question in the format) What the prompt asks it to do per cause, in short: for a conflict, first check whether the base already does what the issue asks (then it ends with --obsolete <sha> , the base's commit, and a one-line why, without redoing the work: once the run ended the dispatcher asks the forge whether that commit is on the base branch; confirmed, the issue gets one note naming the commit and is closed, Gitoodo's own pull request for it too, never set back to ready ; not confirmed, it goes back into the queue and the note says the claim could not be checked, #1574); otherwise rebase onto origin/<base> (merge only where the repository's history is made of merge commits), resolve the conflicts itself (both entries kept in a changelog or list), deliver with gitoodo worker push / pr , which replace the rebased branch on the forge under a lease (see below), and never merge the pre-rebase state back in. It asks only when the two sides want different behaviour, naming every conflicting file and what each side wants. It also reproduces failing checks locally from gitoodo worker context 's failed_checks and ask when the base branch itself is red, read a merge refusal "open dependencies" (412) as a wait and record it with blocked --on , turn a forge dependency, a "defer until #N" answer or a dependency named in the worker's text into blocked --on , and read runs that ended right after their start. Merge rights (405), a release step, a scope decision and the machine's environment are a person's: it asks straight away with the fix. A delivery whose branch lacks the forge's head replaces it with a leased push only when that head is still the one the worker's checkout last saw ( refs/remotes/origin/<branch> ; a satellite sends it with the bundle) and the delivered commit contains the base's current head; anything else is refused as before, so commits someone else pushed are never lost (#1565). gitoodo worker resolved is accepted only from the resolver run itself: through the dispatcher's broker, or on a worker machine through its service, which ends the run and hands the outcome to the dispatcher with the run's end. Outcomes Solved or requeued : the run ends, one collapsed note goes on the issue in the forge's language (the line "the resolver got this issue moving again", unfolded what was stuck, wha

h: What the dispatcher does with it
b: Triage assesses every new, reopened or substantially changed issue once, with one short call to the smallest model of a coding agent the user already has. It sets type, priority and size where nobody set them, records dependencies, asks when information or a decision is missing or the issue looks like a duplicate, and leaves one collapsed note. The dispatcher uses what triage set when it is there and never depends on it: an issue without triage labels is dispatched as before. Code: crates/core/src/triage/ ( output the schema, prompt , fingerprint the hash cache, store the records and budget, plan skip rules, labels and model tiers, agent the call, pass the effects on the forge). The classifier runs a pass per active repository before its reconcile pass ( Writer::triage ), so a new issue is triaged before the intake marks it ready . When an issue is triaged New, reopened or substantially changed. Each issue's text (title and body, without Gitoodo's markers and Depends on lines) has a SHA-256 hash and a small word sketch, stored in triage.json in the state folder. An unchanged hash is never read again. A changed text is triaged again only when less than 80 % of its word triples are the same (a rewritten description, not a typo fix). A closed issue's record is dropped, so a reopened issue is new. Older issues afterwards (#1471). The first pass on a repository reads every open issue as the baseline without a call; issues that come or change afterwards are triaged first. The baseline is then worked through bit by bit: newest first, at most 2 per pass, only after every new issue of the pass is done, only while the agent's usage stays below the user's threshold ( dispatch.usage_threshold_percent , 90 % by default) and, under a daily cap the user chose, with at most three quarters of it, so the rest stays for new issues. Issues a person labelled fully or Gitoodo wrote count as checked without a call. Per repository switch "Triage older issues", on by default ( repos[].triage_backlog ). The progress ( backlog in triage.json : checked, left, why it waited, and since when it runs without a pause with how many done then, for the time left) shows as "assessing older issues · 53 of 141 · ~15 min left". Issues the intake keeps as backlog ( backlog_for ) are left alone. Skipped: pull requests; issues written by workers or Gitoodo (follow-up and part markers, the automation marker); issues a person already labelled fully (a type label or forge issue type and a priority); issues someone works on or that wait ( in-progress , in-review , stalled , needs-human , needs-clarification , extern ). Busy issues are looked at again once they are free. The legacy prd keeps nobody away any more (#1816): a prd issue without dependencies is triaged like any other, and a large one is split there by its worker. Per repository switch. Repository settings → Workers → "Triage new issues", on by default ( orchestration.json → repos[].triage ). Triage runs only while the repository's autopilot is on and nothing is paused. No daily cap by default. Triage stops where the workers stop: at the user's usage threshold ( dispatch.usage_threshold_percent ), for new and older issues alike. A cap is not needed to keep it cheap: each call is a one-shot with the smallest model and a few thousand tokens, and the fingerprint cache never triages an unchanged issue twice, so the calls follow the issues that come or change, not the polls. Three guards stay invisible while nothing goes wrong: Per issue: at most 6 calls per issue and day ( ISSUE_CALLS_PER_DAY ); an issue that keeps coming back is passed over until tomorrow, the others go on ( triage.repeat , once). Runaway: more than 500 calls within an hour ( RUNAWAY_CALLS_PER_HOUR ) means something loops; triage pauses until the next hour ( triage.runaway , once). Only when it trips again for two hours does the status page show it as a fault. Per poll: at most 4 new issues per repository and poll, so a burst spreads over a few polls. Optional cap. AI settings → Advanced → "Triage calls per repository and day": Unlimited (the default), 50, 200, 500 or 1,000 ( settings.json → ai.triage.daily_limit , 0 for unlimited, up to 2,000 in the file; daily_limit_set marks the user's choice). Per account three times that. The former defaults of 25 and 200 were never chosen and read as unlimited unless daily_limit_set says otherwise. A retry counts as a call. When a chosen cap is used up the rest waits for the next day (UTC, triage.budget_exhausted , once per repository and day); the system row and the status page say so with the time it goes on and "Change limit". Agent with capacity. The workers' agent first, then the others, each only when installed and not at its usage limit (the dispatcher's usage cache: a lock in force or a window at 100 %). Without one the pass waits ( triage.no_agent ). Agent that cannot answer (#1407). A call whose agent says it cannot answer any issue now passes that agent over and asks the next one for the same issue in the same pass ( triage.passed_over , kept in triage.json → passed_over ): not signed in ( login , tried again after 15 minutes), at its usage limit ( limit , until the reset its message names, else 30 minutes; Gemini CLI reports no usage ahead, so this is how triage learns of its limit), the triage model unknown or not allowed for the login ( model , an hour, at once with another model chosen) or a CLI without an option of the call ( unsupported , an hour). The cause is read from the agent's own error (its JSON output or stderr), never logged or kept as text. When every installed agent is passed over, the pass waits: at their limits like any agent at its limit, otherwise the status page names the cause and the agent ("Codex is not signed in …"). Any other failure (timeout, an unknown error, an output that is no answer) passes no agent over: the pass stops and the issue comes again on the next poll. Never starved (#1426, #1471). Triage takes no worker slot: a call is a short model call of the classifier without a working copy, so it never waits behind the workers, and the resolver's system slots stay the resolver's. Passes of all repositories and accounts run one after the other in one process (one call at a time), before each repository's reconcile pass, new issues oldest first. The usage threshold and a cap the user chose are the only things that hold it, and both show. State that does not save. Before each call the pass saves triage.json ; when that fails (a full disk) it makes no call ( triage.write_failed , step=store ): a call whose result is not remembered would be made again, with a second note. What did not save is kept in the process and written with the next save. Rewritten during the call. When a person changes the issue's text substantially while its call runs, nothing is written from the answer ( triage.edited ); the new text is triaged on the next pass. A label a person set in the meantime wins: triage only sets what is still unset. The call One non-interactive call with no tools, no MCP servers, no session saved and no repository access (a temporary empty folder as working directory), under the agent's own sign-in: Agent Default model How Claude Code haiku claude -p --output-format json --tools "" with its own short system prompt Codex newest luna codex exec --ephemeral --ignore-user-config -s read-only --json , prompt on stdin Gemini CLI flash-lite gemini --output-format json , prompt on stdin The model per agent is a setting (Settings → AI assist → Advanced → "Triage of new issues"); an empty or unknown value runs the smallest. The call times out after 90 seconds. Calls run one at a time on the dispatcher's computer and take no worker slot (#1426): a call is a short model call without a working copy, so it never waits behind running workers and starts as soon as the classifier gets to the issue, also right after the start ( resolver.md , "System slots"). Input , fenced as data the model must never follow: the title and body (cut at 6,000 characters, about 1,500 tokens), up to 60 other open issues as number and title (newest first), up to 80 label names of the repository, the language to write the free-text fields in (the repository's language on the forge), and the machines workers run on (up to 8): name, system, whether it answers, the agent CLIs ready there and whether workers may use its desktop. The dispatcher, which polls the machines, writes them to worker-machines.json in the state folder when they change; before it has, triage takes this computer and the machines whose system was seen at setup from the configuration ( triage::machines ). Output is one JSON object, checked against a strict schema (unknown fields are refused): Field Values type bug , feature , chore , docs , question priority p0 … p3 , with priority_reason (one sentence) size S , M , L depends_on open issue numbers from the list, only when sure (at most 5) duplicate of , confidence , one-line summaries of both, what overlaps and what differs; or null readiness ready or needs_decision (with 1–3 questions ; each may name the device it is about) worker_decides technical choices the worker makes itself, 0–4 lines An invalid answer gets one retry with the reason (never the answer itself). A second invalid answer ends triage for this text silently: nothing is written to the forge, the record says failed and triage.failed is logged. The same text is not tried again; an edit is. Measured with Claude Haiku on the dev Forgejo: about 1,900 input tokens (part of it cached) and 420 output tokens per issue, about US$0.0004 per issue and 5 seconds per call. What it writes Labels only where no person set one. Per dimension (type, priority, size): a label a person set wins and triage leaves that dimension alone; a label triage set earlier is replaced when the new assessment differs; a triage label a person removed is not set again. Triage remembers the labels it set ( triage.json ), so a later change by a person always wins. It reuses the repository's own names ( bug , Kind/Bug , priority:p1 ) and creates missing type:… , priority:p… and size:… labels. Dependencies through blocked::record_dependency(…, Source::Triage) : a Depends on #N line in the description, a note "Gitoodo's triage found that this issue cannot start before then", and blocked . The classifier makes it ready once the named issues are closed ( dispatcher.md , "Dependencies"). Questions in the question format ( docs/question-format.md ), kind clarification , ids triage-info-… , triage-decision-… and triage-dup-… , addressed to the repository's human (else the author), and needs-human , which holds the issue back from the dispatcher until it is answered. Questions go only to issues of trusted authors (the repository's human or a collaborator with write access); a stranger's issue first goes through the intake's approval. needs_decision : only what a person alone can decide (product, priority or scope, access they control, a trade-off users notice). Each question is checked before it is asked (#1566): it ends in ? , says why it matters (a context line), and has 2–4 options each with its consequence plus a recommendation, or names exactly the one value it needs (a URL, an account), asked as text. An open "what is missing" or "more information" question is never asked, in any language; any other question that fails the check, and every detail the model called missing (the earlier needs_info ), goes to the worker. When no question is left, the issue is ready. Technical details (tool versions to test, formats, test steps) are never a reason to wait: the note lists them as "The worker decides: …", so the worker and every reader see them. A check on a real machine (a test on Windows, macOS or Linux, also in a native app) is a worker's job wherever a worker machine runs that system, also one offline right now: the prompt lists the machines, and a question whose device names such a system goes to the worker and leads

Gitoodo cleans up its own worktrees, branches and temp files: after merges, after crashes and resets, after an uninstall, and above all in the user's own checkouts, which serve as clones since #755. Code: crates/core/src/hygiene/ (decisions, the only removing code), the dispatcher's crates/cli/src/dispatcher_hygiene.rs and the satellite's crates/cli/src/satellite_hygiene.rs . Safety rule In a user checkout Gitoodo only ever runs git worktree remove on worktrees below the worktree root that are its own, git worktree prune , git branch -D <prefix>/<number>… and a fetch of the base. User branches, stashes, the index and working-tree changes of the checkout are never touched ( crates/core/tests/hygiene.rs checks this). Anything that holds work that would be lost (uncommitted files, commits on no remote branch and not in the base by content) is never removed silently; it is reported as a leftover. Ownership Every worktree Gitoodo creates (dispatcher and satellite) gets the marker file gitoodo-owner (JSON: issue key, branch, time, host) in its git folder ( <checkout>/.git/worktrees/<name>/ ), so the working tree stays clean. Its branch is <branch_prefix>/<number>-<title> (default prefix gitoodo ). Older worktrees without a marker count as Gitoodo's when they lie below the worktree root on such a branch. Agent sessions ( agent-session/* ) never match. Reconcile round At dispatcher start (after the leases of the earlier run are released) and every sweep interval (5 min), the dispatcher scans the checkouts of the configured repos, every checkout a folder below worktree_root points to, and the orphan folders there. Before deciding it fetches the base. State Action lease held or worker running (here or on a satellite) keep a "Solve with an agent" session of the issue (#919) keep issue taken: in-progress or assigned (#1813) keep merged (own commits in the base, also after squash), clean remove worktree and local branch issue closed, nothing unsaved remove worktree and local branch issue open, clean and pushed (abandoned) remove worktree, keep branch for a new start waiting for a human ( needs-human , stalled ) or unknown keep unsaved work report as leftover folder deleted by hand worktree prune , branch as above orphan folder: only build output, empty, or files pushed remove the folder orphan folder with files saved nowhere report as leftover, saved by itself (below) Merged needs work of its own (#1813): a fresh branch, cut from the base and never committed to, is an ancestor of the base as well. It counts as merged only when it holds work of its own: commits on no remote branch, or a commit, merge, cherry-pick or revert its reflog records, or a start elsewhere than the base (taken over from the forge's branch). Without a reflog this is unknown and nothing goes as merged; a closed issue still clears it. A branch that only moved along the base stays fresh. A "Solve with an agent" session ( docs/agent-session.md ) works in the issue's worktree without a lease; its record in own-sessions/ keeps the worktree in use until the person closes the tile or hands the issue back. The lease sweep and the cleanup after a merge also delete the local branch once its work is merged or its issue closed. A lease taken between scan and removal wins (checked again right before). Satellites take part on the main host's word: hygiene_scan returns their items, the main host decides with its leases and the forge, hygiene_apply carries the decisions out; a running worker's worktree is refused there too. A backup of a satellite's leftover (#886) runs through hygiene_bundle : the satellite commits the unsaved files and sends the branch beyond the base branch as a git bundle, the main host pushes it as the backup branch with the account's token (satellites hold none) and only then orders the removal. On its own, 30 s after start and every 5 minutes, a satellite sweeps old temp files (also inside the shared sessions folder) and removes what is merged (the scope the main host sent last, kept in satellite-hygiene.json ). It never removes the worktree of an issue the main host holds ( held in the scope: a lease, a run waiting for its restart) or that had a worker there since the main host's last word, and nothing while that word is unknown (#1813). A restart whose worktree is gone (#1813): a worker never starts in a folder that is not there ( PtyWorker::spawn refuses it; the pseudo terminal would fall back to the home folder). A satellite restart without prepare cuts the worktree again from the issue's last prepared start (copy, branch, base). When it cannot (the service restarted since, the copy is gone), it answers "worker worktree is unavailable"; the main host takes that as the issue's own fault, puts the issue back into the queue and its next start comes with prepare , so there is no loop. Leftovers Reported items go to hygiene.json in the state folder ( HygieneStatus ): cleanup state, leftovers with host, issue, branch, commits and uncommitted files, disk reading and errors. Settings › Storage lists the leftovers, beside the automatic cleanup, each with: Discard: removes the worktree and branch with whatever they hold. Push as backup branch and remove: commits uncommitted files, pushes the branch as <prefix>-backup/<rest>-<time> with the account's token, then removes it. On a satellite the main host pushes from the satellite's bundle (#886). The app queues the decision in hygiene-requests.json ; the dispatcher handles it within 5 s and runs a round. dispatch.leftover_expiry_days (default 0 = off) discards leftovers automatically after that many days. gitoodo diagnose lists the leftovers. Saved by itself (#873, #886): the user does not have to decide. A leftover on this host or on a reachable satellite that can be backed up and was first reported an hour ago ( AUTO_BACKUP_SECS ) is pushed as a backup branch and removed in the next round, exactly like "Push as backup branch and remove" ( dispatch.cleanup_auto_backup ). The newest 20 saves are kept in hygiene.json ( saved : issue, branch, time); they need nobody, so no page lists them (#924). A failed push stays a leftover and is tried again next round, marked blocked: failed ; a worktree a worker uses is never touched, and nothing is pushed while Gitoodo is halted. Orphan folders with files saved nowhere are saved the same way (see "Orphan folders"); a satellite that is offline is saved once it is back. Discarding is never automatic unless the expiry is set. Remote branches Hourly, for every configured repo with the sweep rule on, remote <prefix>/* branches without an open pull/merge request, without a lease and without a local branch are deleted once the issue is known (open or closed) and the newer of last commit and first sighting is older than dispatch.remote_branch_grace_hours (default 24, 0 = off). At most 10 per round, one per second, through the forge adapters (Forgejo/Gitea, GitHub, GitLab; every deletion in the forge audit log and the dispatcher log). Disk guard (#771, #970) Code: crates/core/src/hygiene/disk.rs (levels, readings), crates/cli/src/dispatcher_hygiene.rs ( disk_tick ), crates/cli/src/satellite_hygiene.rs ( watch_disk ), crates/cli/src/freeze.rs (pausing a worker's processes). The app sets what stays free for you, the leftover expiry and the remote branch grace in Settings › Storage; the keys stay in the dispatch block of orchestration.json . One space setting (#1809). "Für dich frei halten" ( dispatch.keep_free_gb , "Keep free for you") is the only space setting: a new worker starts only if at least that much stays free after its repository's expected build. Empty is "Automatisch": 15 GiB, or 10 % of a small drive when that is less (so a 100 GiB drive keeps 10 GiB); 0 switches the guard off. Everything else follows from that one value K ( DispatchConfig::disk_guard , disk::Guard ): Derived From K low level (no new worker) K critical level (pause) the smaller of 2 GiB and 1 % of the volume, never above K clean-up starts / frees to below 2 × K / up to 3 × K ( disk::cleanup_bounds ) room for builds free space minus K ( priority::room ); no separate budget unless the file sets a cap The status line under the field says it in one sentence from the dispatcher's last measurement ( storage.json budget : keep_free , room , held ): "Jetzt 165 GB frei, Gitoodos Arbeitskopien belegen 56 GB. Neue Worker starten: Gitoodo nutzt bis zu 150 GB für Builds, 15 GB bleiben für dich frei." While a repository's next build does not fit, it names the repository, its expected build and what is missing. The wait reasons, the status banners and gitoodo diagnose ("builds: Gitoodo may use up to … more, … stay free for you"; "new workers of o/r wait: their build needs about …, … are missing") use the same words. Sizes in GB are GiB, as in the field. Former settings. Before #1809 three values set this: min_free_disk_mb (default 10240), min_free_disk_percent (default 5, the smaller of both counted) and build_budget_gb (0: a fifth of the drive, 20-200 GiB). They are still read, and no installation ends up less protected: Former file Shown as Guard now missing, or the defaults 10240 MiB / 5 % Automatisch 15 GiB / 10 %, never below the old 10 GiB / 5 % on any drive 0 / 0 (off) 0 off a size alone ( M MiB, 0 %) ⌈M / 1024⌉ exactly M MiB, as before a share alone ( 0 MiB, P %) or any other mix Automatisch the larger of automatic and the old level (kept as a floor) build_budget_gb > 0 (not shown) stays a cap on Gitoodo's build output, from the file only build_budget_gb 0 — no cap of its own: the builds may use what is free above K Saving the field writes keep_free_gb and drops the former keys from the file; saving any other field keeps them (and their floor). A satellite gets the resulting levels from the main host ( HygieneScope.min_free_disk_mb / percent , the floor in min_free_floor_mb / percent ), so an older satellite follows the new automatic value too. Every 15 seconds the dispatcher (and every satellite for its own machine) reads the free space of the volume holding worktree_root and, when it differs, of the volume holding Gitoodo's own data (state, logs; the agents' data sits next to it). The free-space reading is cheap ( statvfs , or GetDiskFreeSpaceExW on Windows); sizes of folders are never measured in this loop. Level Begins below Ends at or above Effect low what stays free for you, dispatch.keep_free_gb (automatic: the smaller of 15 GiB and 10 % of the volume) the limit plus a margin no new worker starts on that machine critical the smaller of 2 GiB and 1 % of the volume, never above the low limit the limit plus a margin the machine's running workers are paused as well The margin is a fifth of the limit, at least 1 GiB and at most the limit itself, so a reading that wobbles around a limit does not flap: automatic on a big disk the warning begins below 15 GiB and ends at 18 GiB, the pause begins below 2 GiB and ends at 3 GiB. 0 switches the low limit off (and with it critical ). A volume without a reading (a missing drive, an error) counts as fine and never holds work back. The worst volume sets the machine's level. Low : no new local worker starts (satellites still take work; with none online the dispatch wait reason is disk_low ), DispatcherStatus.disk_low is set and a reconcile round runs. Critical : the running local workers are paused, not stopped: on macOS and Linux their whole process tree gets SIGSTOP (resumed bottom-up with SIGCONT ), on Windows every thread of the tree is suspended ( SuspendThread / ResumeThread ). A paused worker is never counted as hung and its silence starts afresh when it resumes; one that ends during the pause leaves normally, and stopping a paused worker resumes it first so it can exit. They resume on their own once the level drops back to low or ok . Satellites run the same loop for their own disk, refuse a new worker at critical ("the disk of this machine is almost full; free up space there") and report their level in the status r

h: Your repositories' build output (after a confirmation, or when space is short and you switched it on; #1418, #1804)
Scratch folders for checks over ssh (#1680)
b: Coding agents, their tools and their builds fill a disk quickly. Gitoodo frees what can be created again by itself and only suggests what belongs to the user. The engine lives in crates/core/src/autoclean/ (entry point run_automatic_cleanup ), the dispatcher runs it ( crates/cli/src/dispatcher_autoclean.rs ), the Storage page shows it. Satellites run the same engine for their own disk ( crates/cli/src/satellite_autoclean.rs , #1675): the same schedule and low-disk pass, under the main host's settings, with their clones and worktrees as Gitoodo's own (never a tier item) and without the user's repositories, which need a confirmation on the main host. It complements, and never duplicates, the existing cleanup of Gitoodo's own run worktrees ( docs/orchestrator/hygiene.md ): Gitoodo's worktree root, its data and the agents' data of its runs are left to that cleanup and never counted twice. Tiers Tier What When A Fully automatic, silent On its interval B Automatic under conditions On its interval when its conditions hold; in the low-disk pass C Only listed on the Storage page as suggestion Never by itself; an action runs only after a confirmation Tier A Code Item Interval A1 npm cache verify (the tool's own garbage collection) 7 days A2 uv cache prune ( UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT=60 ) 7 days A4 Each local worker gets its own TMPDIR / TEMP / TMP ; removed when its run ends 6 hours A4: the folder is <Gitoodo temp root>/runs/<12 hex characters of the issue key's hash> (owner-only on Unix, short so socket paths stay within the system's limit). It is created when a local worker starts and removed when its lease is released. A folder whose run ended without that (a crash) and that has been idle for an hour is removed by the orphan pass; folders of runs with a lease are never touched. Workers on other machines keep their system temp folder. Tier B Code Item Condition B4 Xcode DerivedData folders Untouched for 7 days (1 when low); Xcode not running B5 Unavailable simulators ( xcrun simctl delete unavailable ) Xcode selected and set up; no simulator booted B7 pnpm store prune 7 days B8 Docker build cache above 20 GB ( docker buildx prune ) Docker answers info ; 7 days. Space inside the Docker VM is not counted as freed on macOS and Windows B9 Gradle caches of old versions, old wrappers 30 days (wrappers 90) B10 NuGet HTTP cache, temp, plugin cache (never global packages) Paths from dotnet nuget locals all --list ; untouched for 30 days B11 Homebrew downloads Files older than 30 days B12 CocoaPods cache Not used for 30 days B13 Dart analysis server byte store Files older than 30 days B14 Go build cache ( go clean -cache ) Only when low B15 Old versions of the coding agent CLI Keeps the current, the newest and the previous one (the previous not when low); not within 24 h of an update (1 h when low) B16 Chromium/Electron app caches ( Cache , GPUCache …) App not running; 30 idle days, or when low B17 Leftover browser code-signing clones (macOS) Older than a day, nothing open inside. They are clones: they free almost nothing and are never shown as large B18 Old temp leftovers of this user; build output in younger temp folders Top-level entries untouched for 7 days, minus sockets and live sessions. Your repositories' build output (after a confirmation, or when space is short and you switched it on; #1418, #1804) The build output of the repositories Gitoodo manages, their linked worktrees and the agent worktrees inside them is the user's: Gitoodo never removes it silently, neither on its interval nor for a low disk ( Item::users_repo ; each pass logs autoclean.skipped with users-repo-needs-confirmation ), unless the user switched on "Remove your repositories' build output automatically when space is short" (Settings → Storage, repo_build_when_short , off by default). Then a pass for short space (a low disk, or builds that wait for room) that has not reached its goal after Gitoodo's own build output and the caches runs once more with Reason::ReposShort for what is still missing ( autoclean.repos_short ; while it is off, autoclean.skipped with item = repos , repo-build-auto-off ): only these items, with the rules and stages of the confirmed removal below, and of them only build output that nothing wrote to for three days ( REPO_BUILD_REST_DAYS ) in a working copy without uncommitted changes ( uncommitted-changes ) that nobody worked in for as long ( used-recently , built-recently ; unknown counts as recent). A build that runs keeps its output as always. Each survey and each pass for a low disk plans what "Remove your repositories' build output" would take ( Reason::Confirmed , plan mode, every check) and keeps the list ( autoclean.json repo_build , largest first). The Storage page offers the action with its total, in the build section and in the warning "Disk almost full"; it asks first and lists every folder. Once confirmed (request id repo_build ), the dispatcher runs it with the low-disk rules and stages below, so nothing a build uses right now goes: Code Item Rule B1 Rust target/ of managed repositories and their worktrees Confirmed by cargo metadata --offline , CACHEDIR.TAG , ignored by git; never a linked target or one cargo does not build into. incremental/ not written in the last 10 minutes, profiles other than the newest not built for a day, the whole folder once nothing was built in it for an hour (never with criterion / package output). Skipped while a build runs in the tree (cargo's lock, a build tool working there) B2 node_modules of managed repositories Manifest, lockfile and install marker, never Plug'n'Play; ignored by git; the worktree untouched for 7 days B3 Framework caches ( .next/cache , .turbo , __pycache__ …) Ignored by git and not tracked; 1 idle day B6 SwiftPM .build/<triple> Ignored by git; 1 idle day It logs autoclean.repo_build_done ( freed ); the list is planned again right after. Each row shows the folder; "Remove" exists only for build output and Xcode device support and asks for a confirmation first. Everything else is only shown in the file manager. Extra worktrees come as a decision ( crates/core/src/autoclean/decide.rs ). The row names what goes and what stays, the facts behind it (branch merged into the base branch, on the server or not pushed; uncommitted changes; unpushed commits; last change as the newest modification time; in use by a process with its working folder or open files there, or named in a running command line; the branch's pull request) and a recommendation. The pull request comes from the forge (#1543): before each survey, and before a confirmed removal, the dispatcher lists the open and the recently merged pull requests of every configured repository once (Forgejo/Gitea, GitHub, GitLab; kept for five minutes). An open pull request with the worktree's branch as its head shows "PR open (#n)" with a link and never lets the working copy go as a whole (the autopilot may still work on it). A merged pull request that ended at the worktree's head counts as merged, also after a squash or rebase merge and with its branch deleted on the server. When the forge could not be asked, the row says "PR state unknown" and the working copy is never advised to go as a whole. The human talks to the orchestrator in a chat that can see and steer the ledger. Architecture The chat runs on the agent picked in the settings (#425, crates/core/src/orchestrator_chat/launch.rs ): Claude Code in stream-json mode, Codex through its app server ( codex app-server , crates/core/src/agent/codex_app.rs , #963) or Gemini CLI over ACP ( gemini --experimental-acp ). Codex and Gemini CLI get the same gitoodo mcp server (narrowed to the scope), the orchestrator instructions and the picked model; they cannot resume a Claude session. For Claude Code the app starts the user's claude in stream-json mode ( --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose ) with --mcp-config pointing to gitoodo mcp . The session runs under the user's subscription. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN are removed from the child environment; no API key is ever used. gitoodo mcp reads the forge with the account tokens, so it runs from the app's service helper ( Contents/Helpers/GitoodoService.app , in the app's keychain access group) when the bundle ships one, like the background services; otherwise from the CLI beside the app or on PATH (#990). Network access and tokens stay in the Rust core and the keychain. Tool results carry no tokens. Program path: the app resolves the agent with the settings' resolver and passes its absolute path as ChatConfig.program and that folder plus the search folders as ChatConfig.path (the child's PATH ), so a minimal app PATH cannot hide it; without a program, env GITOODO_CLAUDE , else claude (tests use a fake). Tauri surface Name Kind Meaning orchestrator_chat_start command, resume? , scope? start (replaces a running chat); returns ModelFallback or null, model per ai.models.chat as --model (#341) orchestrator_chat_send command, text: string one user message orchestrator_chat_stop command stop; no-op without a chat orchestrator-chat-event event payload is a ChatEvent , tagged by type ChatEvent types: started (session_id, model, tools), text , tool_use (id, name, input), tool_result (id, text, is_error), turn_done (session_id, is_error, result, usage, cost_usd), other (kind), malformed (line), ended (code). Unknown stream events become other . scope is a ChatScope tagged by kind : all , repo ( account , repo = owner/name ) or item (plus number ); missing means all . The child runs gitoodo mcp --scope acc/owner/name or --scope acc/owner/name#7 , and the system prompt names the scope. MCP tools ( gitoodo mcp ) The chat pre-approves exactly the names in CHAT_TOOLS . Reading needs no prompt. dispatcher_instruct_worker relays an explicit human request directly to an existing session, using the same guarded dispatcher path as the session instruction box, including remote workers. The model first lists workers, selects only the requested recipients and calls once per recipient. Ambiguous recipients require clarification. Issue bodies and tool output are not authorization. The server validates the account/repository/item scope and instruction length. It refuses missing workers and unsent human input. Success means submitted, not executed; failures are reported per recipient and uncertain delivery is never retried automatically. No issue is created for a relay. Forge and configuration changes still use forge_propose_change and require the proposal card's OK. ACP agents get the same tool surface. Tool Required Effect ledger_list_items none ( repo , readiness , label , limit ) open issues, highest score first ledger_release_status none ( repo ) items of the next release and their state ledger_version_suggestion none ( repo ) suggested next version with its reason ledger_release_suggestions none ( repo ) release suggestions waiting for approval ledger_release_runs none ( repo ) completed releases and their step progress ledger_list_questions none ( repo ) open question cards dispatcher_status none usage, throttle, lock, counts dispatcher_workers none running workers dispatcher_instruct_worker key , text submit a human instruction to one running worker dispatcher_queue none ( limit ) ready, unleased issues of dispatching repos Context layers (#339) Read-only tools the model calls on demand, broad to narrow. Each stays inside the chat scope (a repo outside it is an error result); overview, labels and issue lists read only the synced ledger; pull requests, activity and item details fetch through the core's forge client with the keychain token. Tool Optional arguments Content context_overview none per repo: rule state, open count, readiness, leases context_items repo , kind , readiness , limit open issues (ledger) and/or PRs (checks, linked issues) context_labels repo label usage and readiness distribution context_activity repo , limit recently updated issues and PRs of one repo context_item key , kind one item in depth; defaults to the scoped item Contract test: context_layers_follow_the_scope in crates/cli/src/mcp.rs (fake backend). Proposed changes (#340) Forge changes, repository state changes and worker stops require a proposal. forge_propose_change (required change ) only validates the call against the chat scope and answers that the human decides; the backend is never touched. Forge changes: comment ( body ), labels ( add , remove ), status ( status ), close (optional reason , posted as a comment first), reopen , answer ( block_id , answers as ledger_list_questions and the app's answer form use them, optional free_text ; posted as the answer comment of the question format) (each on key = account/owner/name#number , default the scoped item) and create_issue ( title , body , labels , on account + repo , default the scoped repo). Gitoodo's own state: pause_repo and resume_repo (on account + repo , default the scoped repo; only between active and paused ) and stop_worker (on key ; parks the worker without a restart, the issue keeps its lease). A new repository (#1654): create_repo ( account + repo = owner/name , default account the scoped one; private , default true ; optional folder , ~ allowed; autopilot , default false ). It is the only change outside the chat scope, since the repository does not exist yet; the human's OK decides. Its card shows what the app's "New project" would do ( setup in the ProposalView : the repo setup plan and the folder check, see repo-setup.md ), and the OK runs exactly that path: create on the recommended profile, push the folder's files or clone into an empty folder, then turn the repository on ( paused , active with autopilot ) with the folder as its working copy. A folder that is refused or holds secret-looking files keeps the OK disabled; only the "New project" page lets the person confirm such files. The result links to the new repository; a failed step names its step, error and git's message. Earlier, these three and the answer were direct tools ( ledger_answer_question , ledger_set_repo_state , dispatcher_stop_worker ) that ran without the human's OK; they are gone. The app records every accepted call in a ProposalBook ( crates/core/src/orchestrator_chat/ proposal.rs ), keyed by the tool call id; a call with an error result is dropped again. Commands: orchestrator_chat_proposal(id) → ProposalView ( proposal , state , preview with the item's title and before / after state and labels, preview_error ; reads only), orchestrator_chat_proposal_apply(id) → ProposalState , orchestrator_chat_proposal_discard(id) . state.phase : pending → applying → applied ( link , the forge's page of the result) or failed ( error ); pending → discarded . Apply and discard work only from pending ; a second OK is refused with proposal_settled , an unknown id with proposal_unknown . A failed write is not retried; the model may propose again. An applied create_issue is written with the chat's account (the human's connected account and token), so it is an ordinary issue by that author: the classifier's intake (spec 5.3) makes it ready when the author is trusted and the body is complete, exactly like an issue the human wrote on the forge or with "New issue" on the board. The OK on the card is the only confirmation; there is no second approval. Writes go through the same paths as the app's buttons: forge changes through the core's forge write paths, an answer through the answer path on the open question card (the card must still be open; the preview shows the exact comment), pausing and resuming through the repository state (orchestrator mode only) and stopping through the dispatcher's park request ( confirm_with in proposal.rs ). Error texts are passed through secret redaction and lose any user:pass@ part of URLs. Local changes report no link. Direct mode hides the tab; switching to direct mode while the chat shows moves to the overview ( src/views/shell/tabs.ts ). The conversation and the unsent draft live in a module store ( src/views/dashboard/chatStore.ts ) that follows the events for the app's lifetime; switching tabs keeps the session running until it is stopped. src/views/dashboard/chat.ts is the pure reducer from ChatEvent s plus local actions to entries (user, assistant, tool row, turn error) and phases idle , starting , ready , busy , ended , failed . Changing the scope while the chat runs restarts it with resume , so the conversation stays but a running turn is cut; when stopped, the next start uses the new scope.
